441	do not rely on DNA at all, and they bring reasoning instead. And so, huh?
442	It helps with the testing, it helps. So that's it. I wanted to say that for extra clarity it is possible to bring DNA,
443	but they said no, even for extra clarity they don't rely on it at all. It doesn't matter to me, even if it would help me support
444	my ruling, I don't bring DNA at all. They don't bring DNA. So I wanted to write in my responsa,
445	in the conclusion, "and for extra clarity I permit DNA together with reasoning in the way of the Torah."
446	I changed my mind. I changed my mind and said: no, I permit reasoning in the way of the Torah
447	with the addition of DNA.
448	Is there a difference?
449	Certainly.
450	Someone once came to his rabbi and said, "Rabbi, when I learn Torah, may I smoke?"
451	The rabbi told him, "No, you may not smoke. When you learn Torah, you don't smoke."
452	He went to his friend and said, "Listen, I asked the rabbi, and the rabbi said that when you learn Torah you don't smoke."
453	He said to him, "Why are you so naive? You don't know how to ask. Come with me."
454	He went to the rabbi and said, "Rabbi, when I smoke, may I learn Torah?"
455	He said to him, "Of course. When you smoke, you may learn Torah. But when you learn Torah, you may not smoke."
456	Is there a difference?
457	It depends how you present it. It depends how you present it.
458	When you learn Torah you can't smoke, but when you smoke you can learn Torah. Why not?
459	It's permitted, no problem. What's the point?
460	It depends how you phrase it. Here too, at first I wrote that I permit DNA
461	with the addition of reasoning of the Torah, in the way of the Torah. Then I changed my mind and said: no, I permit reasoning in the way
462	of the Torah, and for extra clarity one may add the DNA. What do you say?
